walk/bowl: Here is the bowl from the gradient, f of u and v is u squared plus two v squared, seen from above, with a point at one, one. The task now: get to the bottom, where f is smallest.
walk/fog: This bowl can be seen whole. A function of thousands of inputs cannot be drawn, so all you can learn is how it slopes right where you stand, like a walker in thick fog who feels only the ground underfoot.
walk/down: That is enough to choose a direction. The gradient, two, four, points straight uphill, so head the opposite way, along minus two, minus four: straight downhill.
walk/short: But go only a short way, since the slope you felt holds only near your feet. Take a small step, then feel the slope again where you land.
walk/walk: Step after step, each one straight downhill from wherever you stand, the walk winds its way to the bottom.
walk/cauchy: Augustin-Louis Cauchy proposed this walk in 1847. Working out the orbit of a heavenly body meant solving many equations at once, so he folded them into one function to make small, and stepped against its slopes.
rule/w: Now give things names. Gather the inputs into one vector, w, for where you stand: here, one, one.
rule/g: Call the gradient at w just g: two, four.
rule/eta: How far to step is set by a small positive number, eta, the Greek letter eta, called the step size. Here it is zero point one.
rule/eg: The step goes against g, scaled by eta. Eta times g is zero point two, zero point four: the gradient, cut to a tenth.
rule/new: Subtract that from w, entry by entry, and w becomes zero point eight, zero point six: one step down the bowl.
rule/rule: That is the whole rule, written w gets w minus eta g. The arrow reads “gets”: the new w is the old w, minus eta times g.
rule/sign: Each entry moves against its own slope. From minus one, one, the gradient is minus two, four. Subtracting eta times minus two adds, so u moves right, toward the bottom, while v moves down.
rule/which: So the sign of each entry of g decides which way that entry of w goes. Eta is always positive: it sets how far, never which way.
rule/steep: And twice the slope makes twice the step. Near the bottom the bowl flattens, g shrinks, and the steps shrink on their own.
drop/ask: How much lower is f after that step? The gradient answers this too: a small move changes f by about each slope times its move, added up.
drop/each: Each entry moved by minus eta times its own slope. Times that slope again, its share of the change is minus eta times its slope squared.
drop/never: A square is never negative, written g of i, squared, is at least zero, where the sign in the middle reads “is at least”. So every share is a drop.
drop/works: That is why the rule works: a small enough step never raises f. Cauchy wrote down this same estimate in 1847.
drop/sum: Here, two squared plus four squared is twenty.
drop/est: Times minus eta, which is minus zero point one: f should drop by about two.
drop/true: In fact, the new f is one point three six, down from three: a drop of one point six four. Close, and closer still for a smaller step.
